## A different question this time

Posts 3 and 4 both asked the same kind of question: can a small local VLM *generate* a correct
label — defect or not, and where — from scratch? Answer, twice now: detection improves with
fine-tuning, localization doesn't, in two different specific ways depending on the model.

This post asks something more practical, and honestly closer to a problem I actually run into: I
have automated labeling pipelines that get it right most of the time — call it 95% — and wrong the
rest. Instead of asking a small model to produce the label, what if I ask it to **grade** a label
someone (or something) else already produced? That's a strictly easier task in principle —
verification instead of generation — and it maps directly onto a real use case: a cheap second
pass that flags the suspicious 5% for a human, instead of a human reviewing everything.

Short version: **few-shot examples nearly doubled the judge's recall overall, at higher precision,
not lower — genuinely the cleanest win this series has produced. And it did that by getting much
better at one error type while going to a flat 0% on another, more dangerous one. I dug into why,
and the answer is more mundane and more useful than I expected.**

## The setup

Show the model one image plus a *proposed* label — `defect: true/false`, with the proposed box
drawn directly on the image in yellow when it claims a defect — and ask for a verdict:

```
{"verdict": "correct"} or {"verdict": "incorrect"}
```

Outlines-constrained generation, same pattern as posts 3/4, so there's no parsing free text out of
a maybe-malformed response.

GDXray's real labels are all correct, obviously — there's no natural pool of real auto-labeler
mistakes sitting in a research dataset. So I built synthetic ones, and I want to be upfront about
that rather than bury it: errors here are injected, not real auto-labeling failures. Three kinds:

- **classification_flip_fp** — a real `no_defect` image relabeled `defect`, with a box borrowed
  from a real defect elsewhere in the dataset and rescaled to fit, so it looks like a plausible
  mistake instead of an obviously empty one.
- **classification_flip_fn** — a real `defect` image relabeled `no_defect`, box dropped.
- **localization_shift** — label stays `defect: true`, but the box gets replaced with one moved to
  IoU<0.1 against the real box. Same size, wrong place.

Eval set: post 3/4's exact 668-image eval split (byte-identical manifest, same series-level
train/eval boundary), corrupted at roughly 50/50 so precision and recall stay meaningful instead
of getting swamped by class imbalance the way plain accuracy did in every earlier post in this
series. Actual composition landed at 49.0% correct / 51.0% corrupted — close enough to call
balanced. One honest caveat up front: because only 131 of the 668 eval images are real defects,
the two corruption types that need a defect image to start from — flip_fn and localization_shift —
only have 37 and 32 examples respectively. Those two breakdowns carry noticeably more noise than
the headline number.

## Few-shot demos

Four fixed examples, pulled from the *train* split only (no eval leakage): 1 correct-defect
example, 1 correct-no_defect example, 1 incorrect classification_flip_fp example, 1 incorrect
localization_shift example. I picked these up front, before running anything, on the assumption
that covering "a wrong yes" and "a wrong box" would give the model enough of a sense of what
"incorrect" looks like. That assumption turned out to matter a lot more than I expected — more on
that below.

## Results

| | accuracy | precision | recall |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zero-shot | 59.7% | 82.1% | 27.0% |
| Few-shot | 72.8% | 93.0% | **50.4%** |

I'll be honest, this is a better result than I expected going in. Four in-context examples nearly
doubled recall (27.0% → 50.4%) *and* improved precision (82.1% → 93.0%) — not a
precision-for-recall trade like every fine-tuning result in posts 3 and 4, an improvement on both
axes at once. If this were the whole story, it'd be the most unambiguously positive result in the
series so far.

It's not the whole story.

### Recall by corruption type

| corruption type | n | zero-shot recall | few-shot recall |
|---|---|---|---|
| classification_flip_fp (false "defect" claim) | 272 | 25.7% | **58.1%** |
| classification_flip_fn (missed real defect) | 37 | 5.4% | **0.0%** |
| localization_shift (wrong box) | 32 | **62.5%** | 43.8% |

Break the aggregate number apart and it's a completely different picture. Few-shot helped
enormously on catching false "defect" claims — more than doubled that recall. But on
classification_flip_fn — a real defect mislabeled as clean, the single most dangerous error type
in an actual QA setting, the one you'd most want a safety-net judge to catch — few-shot recall
went to **exactly 0 out of 37**. Not "worse." Zero. And it wasn't great zero-shot either (5.4%),
but zero-shot at least caught 2.

I noticed the aggregate number first, felt genuinely good about it for about a minute, then broke
it down by corruption type and felt a lot less good. This is exactly the kind of result this
series exists to report honestly rather than round off.

### I checked why — and this one has a clean, specific answer

A flat 0/37 is either a real ceiling or an artifact of how I built the eval, and by now I've
learned not to trust a suspiciously clean number without checking. I went back to the four
few-shot demos:

| demo | proposed `defect` | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `true` | correct |
| 2 | `false` | correct |
| 3 | `true` | incorrect |
| 4 | `true` | incorrect |

Every single "incorrect" demonstration I picked has `proposed_defect: true` — a wrong "yes" or a
wrong box. Not one demo shows the model that a `defect: false` claim, with no box on screen, can
also be wrong. In few-shot mode, the model apparently picked up "no box shown → probably fine" as
a shortcut reinforced by exactly the examples I gave it, and applied it to every single one of the
37 real defects that got relabeled clean.

![A real defect (this image is genuinely `defect: true` in GDXray), relabeled `no_defect` — no box shown. The few-shot judge said `correct`. Every one of the 37 images in this exact situation got the same wrong answer.](images/judge-fewshot-flip-fn-miss.png)

That's a real, fixable gap in how I built the demo set, not necessarily a hard ceiling on the
task. I didn't retest with a 5th demo covering this exact case before writing this up — I'd rather
report the honest result of the demo set I actually committed to up front than go back and
cherry-pick a fix after seeing where it failed. But I'd bet on it mattering: adding one
demonstration of "no box shown, still wrong" is the obvious next experiment, and I'd be surprised
if it didn't move that 0% by a meaningful amount.

The localization_shift regression (62.5% → 43.8%) I'm less confident reading anything into — n=32
means that's a 20-vs-14 split, well within the range I'd expect from noise alone on a set this
small. Flagging it rather than either explaining it away or building a story on top of it.

### And a genuine win, to be fair to the result

Not every corrupted label is subtle. Here's one the few-shot judge caught cleanly — a real
`no_defect` casting, relabeled `defect` with a borrowed box that doesn't correspond to anything
actually wrong with the part:

![A real `no_defect` image, relabeled `defect` with a box borrowed from elsewhere in the dataset. The few-shot judge correctly said `incorrect`.](images/judge-fewshot-flip-fp-catch.png)

272 of the 668 eval rows are this exact corruption type, and few-shot recall on it — 58.1% — is
the best number in this entire post. If your auto-labeling pipeline's failure mode looks more like
"occasionally invents a defect that isn't there" than "occasionally misses a real one," this
result is genuinely encouraging.

## So — does it make sense as a real QA step?

My honest read: **partially, and the part that works isn't the part I'd have guessed mattered
most going in.** A few-shot judge built this way is decent — not great, but decent — at catching
false alarms. It is currently unsafe to rely on for catching missed defects, which is the failure
mode that actually matters if you're trying to keep bad parts from shipping. I don't think that's
a fundamental property of the task, given how directly it traces back to a gap in four
hand-picked examples rather than to the model running into a wall — but I also don't want to
claim it's fixed until I've actually rerun it with a better demo set and can show a number.

If I were deploying something like this for real, today, based only on what's in this post: I'd
use it as a first-pass filter for "does this look like a false positive," not as a substitute for
human review on "did we miss something real." Those are very different reliability bars, and this
experiment shows they're not the same task even though they look like the same task on paper.

## What's next

The obvious immediate follow-up: add a 5th few-shot demo — a real defect relabeled `no_defect`,
verdict `incorrect` — and see whether that flat 0% actually moves, or whether something deeper is
going on. If it does move, that's a strong, useful finding about how sensitive few-shot judging is
to demo *coverage*, not just demo *count*. If it doesn't, that's an even more interesting finding.

Beyond that: this post deliberately stayed at prompting only, no fine-tuning, because that's the
question that was actually asked. Whether a LoRA-tuned judge closes the classification_flip_fn gap
faster or more reliably than a 5th demo would is the natural next comparison — and ties back
directly to posts 3/4's finding that detection-shaped tasks are the ones that respond to
fine-tuning in this series so far.
